props.title: Abbott and Costello Meet the Mummy
props.initialSlug: Comedy duo faces mayhem with ancient Egyptian monster

sections.content: Abbott and Costello Meet the Mummy (1955) marks the final Universal Pictures collaboration for comedy legends Bud Abbott and Lou Costello, capping their successful run of horror-comedy mashups that began with Abbott and Costello Meet Frankenstein (1948). This entry perfectly exemplifies the duo's signature blend of vaudeville slapstick with monster movie tropes, following their established formula of mixing scared-silly routines with genuine Universal horror atmosphere. While not as groundbreaking as their Frankenstein meeting or as tightly crafted as Abbott and Costello Meet the Invisible Man (1951), it delivers memorable sequences like the burger-eating mummy hand gag and the multiple-medallion chase.

sections.content: The film represents a fascinating intersection between two dying breeds of cinema - the classic Universal monster movies and old-school vaudeville comedy. By 1955, both genres were facing extinction as audience tastes shifted toward atomic age sci-fi like Them! (1954) and more sophisticated comedy styles. Yet Abbott and Costello's practiced routines still spark genuine laughs, while the Egyptian setting provides exotic atmosphere despite the obvious budget constraints. The film's broad humor and simplified plot actually work in its favor, making it more accessible than some of Universal's later serious mummy films like The Mummy's Curse (1944).

While modern viewers might find the effects dated and the comedy broad, Abbott and Costello Meet the Mummy maintains historical significance as the last gasp of Universal's original monster cycle before shifting to creature features like Tarantula (1955) and The Creature Walks Among Us (1956). The film also demonstrates how horror-comedy evolved from the sophisticated wit of The Cat and the Canary (1939) to more slapstick-oriented fare, paving the way for later entries like The Ghost and Mr. Chicken (1966). sections.content: Abbott and Costello's monster meetings helped establish a template for horror-comedy that influenced decades of films. Their successful formula of mixing genuine scares with broad comedy can be seen in everything from Young Frankenstein (1974) to Shaun of the Dead (2004). The duo's approach of treating the monsters seriously while reacting with comic terror created a blueprint that later films like The Monster Squad (1987) and Scary Movie (2000) would both embrace and subvert.
